danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Den syttende august red Rostov og Iljin, ledsaget af Lavrusjka, der netop var vendt tilbage fra fangenskab, og en husarordonnans, af sted fra deres kvarter i Jankovo, halvanden mil fra Bogutjarovo, for at prøve en ny hest, som Iljin havde købt, og for at finde ud af, om der var hø at opdrive i landsbyerne.

I tre dage havde Bogutjarovo ligget mellem de to fjendtlige hære, så det var lige så let for den russiske bagtrop at nå dertil som for den franske fortrop; Rostov (Nikolaj) ønskede som omhyggelig eskadronschef at sikre de forsyninger, der stadig fandtes i Bogutjarovo, før franskmændene kunne nå dem.

Rostov og Iljin var i det bedste humør. På vej til Bogutjarovo — et fyrsteligt gods med herregård og avlsgård, hvor de håbede at finde mange husslaver og smukke piger — spurgte de Lavrusjka ud om Napoleon og lo af hans historier og kappedes om at prøve Iljins hest.
Rostov anede ikke, at den landsby, han red ind i, tilhørte netop den Bolkonskij, der havde været forlovet med hans søster.
Rostov og Iljin gav deres heste frie tøjler til et sidste kapløb ned ad skråningen mod Bogutjarovo, og Rostov, der overhentede Iljin, var den første, der galoperede ind på landsbyens gade.
»Du er først!« råbte Iljin med røde kinder.
»Ja, altid først — både på engen og her,« svarede Rostov og klappede sin ophidsede don-hest.
»Og jeg ville have vundet på min franske, Deres Excellence,« sagde Lavrusjka bagfra med hentydning til sin lurvede arbejdshest, »men jeg ville bare ikke ydmyge Dem.«
De red i skridtgang hen til laden, hvor en stor skare bønder stod samlet.

Nogle af mændene blottede hovedet, andre stirrede på de nyankomne uden at tage huen af. To høje, gamle bønder med rynkede ansigter og tyndt skæg kom ud fra kroen, smilende, vaklende og syngende en usammenhængende sang, og nærmede sig officererne.
»Flotte karle!« sagde Rostov leende. »Er der noget hø her?«
»Og hvor de ligner hinanden,« sagde Iljin.
»Et m-e-e-get m-u-u-ntert se-e-lskab...!« sang den ene bonde med et saligt smil.
En af mændene trådte ud af mængden og gik hen til Rostov.
»Hvem tilhører I?« spurgte han.
»Franskmændene,« svarede Iljin spøgende, »og her er Napoleon selv« — og han pegede på Lavrusjka.
»Så I er russere?« spurgte bonden igen.
»Og er I mange her?« sagde en anden, en lille mand, der kom hen til dem.
»Rigtig mange,« svarede Rostov. »Men hvorfor er I samlet her?« tilføjede han. »Er det en helligdag?«
»De gamle er samlet for at drøfte kommunens anliggender,« svarede bonden og trådte til side.
I det øjeblik sås på vejen fra den store gård to kvinder og en mand i hvid hat komme gående mod officererne.
»Hende i lyserødt er min, så hold jer væk!« sagde Iljin, da han så Dunjasja komme løbende resolut mod ham.
»Hun bliver vores!« sagde Lavrusjka til Iljin og blinkede.
»Hvad ønsker I, min søde?« sagde Iljin med et smil.
»Fyrstinden bad mig spørge om jeres regiment og jeres navn.«
»Dette er grev Rostov, eskadronschef, og jeg er jeres ydmyge tjener.«
»Se-e-lskab!« brølte den berusede bonde med et saligt smil, mens han så på Iljin, der talte med pigen. Efter Dunjasja kom Alpatytj hen til Rostov; han havde blottet hovedet allerede på afstand.

»Tør jeg fordriste mig til at besvære Deres ære?« sagde han ærbødigt, men med et anstrøg af foragt for denne officers ungdom og med en hånd stukket ind på brystet. »Min frue, datter af generalløjtnant fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij, som døde den femtende i denne måned, befinder sig i vanskeligheder på grund af disse menneskers grovhed« — han pegede på bønderne — »og beder Dem komme op til huset.... Vær venlig at ride lidt længere frem,« sagde Alpatytj med et melankolsk smil, »da det ikke er bekvemt i nærheden af...« Han pegede på de to bønder, der holdt sig lige så tæt på ham som hestefluer på en hest.
»Ah!... Alpatytj... Ah, Jakov Alpatytj... Storslået! Tilgiv os for Kristi skyld, hva'?« sagde bønderne og smilede fornøjet til ham.
Rostov så på de berusede bønder og smilede.
»Eller underholder de måske Deres ære?« bemærkede Alpatytj med en alvorlig mine, idet han pegede på de gamle mænd med sin frie hånd.
»Nej, der er ikke meget at more sig over her,« sagde Rostov og red et lille stykke videre. »Hvad er der sket?« spurgte han.

»Jeg tillader mig at oplyse Deres ære om, at de uhøflige bønder her ikke vil lade fruen forlade godset og truer med at spænde hestene fra, så selvom alt har været pakket siden morgen, kan Hendes Excellence ikke komme af sted.«
»Umuligt!« udbrød Rostov.
»Jeg har den ære at berette den rene sandhed,« sagde Alpatytj.

Rostov steg af hesten, overlod den til ordonansen og fulgte Alpatytj til huset, mens han spurgte til forholdene. Det viste sig, at fyrstindens tilbud om korn til bønderne dagen før og hendes samtale med Dron og ved mødet faktisk havde haft en så dårlig virkning, at Dron til sidst havde opgivet nøglerne og sluttet sig til bønderne og ikke var dukket op, da Alpatytj sendte bud efter ham; og at om morgenen, da fyrstinden gav ordre til at spænde for til sin rejse, var bønderne kommet i stor skare til laden og havde sendt bud om, at de ikke ville lade hende forlade landsbyen: der var en ordre om ikke at flytte sig, og de ville spænde hestene fra. Alpatytj var gået ud for at tale dem til rette, men fik at vide (det var hovedsagelig Karp, der førte ordet, mens Dron holdt sig i baggrunden) at de ikke kunne lade fyrstinden rejse, at der var en modstridende ordre, men at hvis hun blev, ville de tjene hende som før og adlyde hende i alt.

I det øjeblik, da Rostov og Iljin galopperede ned ad vejen, havde fyrstinde Marja trods Alpatytjs, ammens og pigernes fraråden givet ordre til at spænde for og agtede at tage af sted, men da rytterne blev set, tog man dem for franskmænd, kusken løb sin vej, og kvinderne i huset begyndte at jamre.
»Fader! Velgører! Gud har sendt jer!« lød dybt bevægede stemmer, da Rostov gik gennem forstuen.

Fyrstinde Marja sad hjælpeløs og forvirret i den store stue, da Rostov blev vist ind. Hun kunne ikke fatte, hvem han var, hvorfor han var kommet, eller hvad der skete med hende. Da hun så hans russiske ansigt og i hans gang og hans første ord genkendte en mand af hendes egen stand, så hun på ham med sit dybe, strålende blik og begyndte at tale med en stemme, der skælvede og dirrede af følelse. Dette møde slog straks Rostov som en romantisk begivenhed. »En hjælpeløs pige, overvældet af sorg, overladt til grove, oprørske bønders nåde! Og hvilken mærkelig skæbne sendte mig herhen! Hvilken blødhed og adel der er i hendes træk og udtryk!« tænkte han, mens han betragtede hende og lyttede til hendes forsagte beretning.

Da hun begyndte at fortælle ham, at alt dette var sket dagen efter hendes fars begravelse, skælvede hendes stemme. Hun vendte sig bort, og da hun frygtede, at han ville opfatte hendes ord som beregnet på at vække hans medlidenhed, så hun på ham med et ængsteligt, spørgende blik. Der var tårer i Rostovs øjne. Fyrstinde Marja lagde mærke til det og så taknemmeligt på ham med det strålende blik, der fik hendes ansigts lidenhed til at gå i glemme.

»Jeg kan ikke udtrykke, fyrstinde, hvor glad jeg er for, at jeg tilfældigt red herhen og kan vise min vilje til at tjene Dem,« sagde Rostov og rejste sig. »Tag af sted, når det passer Dem, og jeg giver Dem mit æresord på, at ingen skal fordriste sig til at forurolige Dem, blot De vil tillade mig at tjene som Deres eskorte.« Og med en ærbødig bøjning, som til en kvinde af kongelig byrd, gik han mod døren.
Rostovs respektfulde tone syntes at antyde, at selvom han ville betragte sig som lykkelig over at stifte bekendtskab med hende, ønskede han ikke at udnytte hendes ulykke til at trænge sig på.
Fyrstinde Marja forstod dette og satte pris på hans taktfuldhed.
»Jeg er Dem meget, meget taknemmelig,« sagde hun på fransk, »men jeg håber, at det hele var en misforståelse, og at ingen bærer skylden for det.« Hun begyndte pludselig at græde.
»Undskyld!« sagde hun.
Rostov rynkede brynene og forlod rummet med endnu en dyb bøjning.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: On the seventeenth of August, Rostov and Ilyin, accompanied by Lavrushka, who had just returned from captivity, and a hussar orderly, left their quarters at Yankovo—ten miles from Bogucharovo—and went for a ride to try out a new horse Ilyin had bought and to find out whether there was any hay to be had in the villages.

For the last three days Bogucharovo had lain between the two hostile armies, so it was as easy for the Russian rearguard to reach it as for the French vanguard. Rostov, as a careful squadron commander, wanted to take whatever provisions remained at Bogucharovo before the French could get them.

Rostov and Ilyin were in the merriest of moods. On the way to Bogucharovo—a princely estate with a manor house and farm where they hoped to find many household servants and pretty girls—they questioned Lavrushka about Napoleon and laughed at his stories, and raced each other to try out Ilyin's horse.
Rostov had no idea that the village he was riding into was the property of that same Bolkonsky who had been engaged to his sister.
Rostov and Ilyin gave their horses free rein for one last race along the slope before reaching Bogucharovo, and Rostov, outpacing Ilyin, was the first to gallop into the village street.
"You're first!" cried Ilyin, flushed.
"Yes, always first—on the grass and here," answered Rostov, stroking his heated Don horse.
"And I'd have won on my Frenchie, your excellency," said Lavrushka from behind, referring to his scruffy cart horse, "only I didn't want to embarrass you."
They rode at a walk to the barn, where a large crowd of peasants stood.

Some of the men bared their heads; others stared at the newcomers without removing their caps. Two tall old peasants with wrinkled faces and thin beards emerged from the tavern, smiling, staggering, and singing some slurred song, and approached the officers.
"Fine fellows!" said Rostov, laughing. "Is there any hay here?"
"And how alike they look," said Ilyin.
"A mo-o-ost me-rr-ry com-pa..." sang one of the peasants with a blissful smile.
One man came out of the crowd and went up to Rostov.
"Who do you belong to?" he asked.
"The French," replied Ilyin jokingly. "And here's Napoleon himself"—and he pointed to Lavrushka.
"So you're Russians?" the peasant asked again.
"And is there a large force of you here?" said another, a short man, coming up.
"Quite large," answered Rostov. "But why have you all gathered here?" he added. "Is it a holiday?"
"The old men have met to discuss village business," replied the peasant, moving away.
At that moment, on the road leading from the manor house, two women and a man in a white hat were seen coming toward the officers.
"The one in pink is mine—hands off!" said Ilyin, spotting Dunyasha running determinedly toward him.
"She'll be ours!" said Lavrushka to Ilyin with a wink.
"What do you want, pretty girl?" said Ilyin with a smile.
"The princess ordered me to ask your regiment and your name."
"This is Count Rostov, squadron commander, and I am your humble servant."
"Co-o-om-pa-ny!" roared the tipsy peasant with a blissful smile, watching Ilyin talk to the girl. Following Dunyasha, Alpatych advanced toward Rostov, having bared his head while still at a distance.

"May I make bold to trouble your honor?" he said respectfully, but with a shade of contempt for the youthfulness of this officer, with one hand inside his coat. "My mistress, the daughter of General-in-Chief Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky, who died on the fifteenth of this month, finding herself in difficulty because of the behavior of these people"—he pointed to the peasants—"asks you to come up to the house... Won't you please ride on a little farther," said Alpatych with a melancholy smile, "as it's not convenient in the presence of..." He indicated the two peasants who hovered near him like horseflies around a horse.
"Ah!... Alpatych... Ah, Yakov Alpatych... Such fun! Forgive us for Christ's sake, eh?" said the peasants, grinning happily at him.
Rostov looked at the tipsy peasants and smiled.
"Or perhaps they amuse your honor?" remarked Alpatych with a straight face, pointing at the old men with his free hand.
"No, there's not much to be amused at here," said Rostov, and rode on a little. "What's the matter?" he asked.

"I must inform your honor that the crude peasants here refuse to let the mistress leave the estate and threaten to unhitch her horses, so that although everything has been packed since this morning, her excellency cannot get away."
"Impossible!" exclaimed Rostov.
"I have the honor of reporting the actual truth," said Alpatych.

Rostov dismounted, gave his horse to the orderly, and followed Alpatych to the house, questioning him about the situation. It turned out that the princess's offer of grain to the peasants the day before, her talk with Dron and at the meeting, had actually had such a bad effect that Dron had finally given up the keys, joined the peasants, and hadn't appeared when Alpatych sent for him; and that in the morning when the princess gave orders to harness for the journey, the peasants had come in a large crowd to the barn and sent word that they would not let her leave the village, that there were orders not to move, and that they would unhitch the horses. Alpatych had gone out to reason with them but was told (it was mainly Karp who did the talking, with Dron staying out of sight) that they couldn't let the princess go, that there was an order against it, but that if she stayed they would serve her as before and obey her in everything.

At the moment when Rostov and Ilyin were galloping down the road, Princess Mary, despite Alpatych's protests, her nurse's warnings, and the maids' pleas, had given orders to harness and intended to leave. But when the cavalrymen were spotted, they were mistaken for Frenchmen; the coachman ran away, and the women in the house began to wail.
"Father! Benefactor! God has sent you!" cried deeply moved voices as Rostov passed through the entrance hall.

Princess Mary was sitting helpless and bewildered in the large sitting room when Rostov was shown in. She couldn't grasp who he was or why he had come, or what was happening to her. When she saw his Russian face, and by his walk and his first words recognized him as a man of her own class, she looked at him with her deep, radiant gaze and began speaking in a voice that faltered and trembled with emotion. To Rostov, this meeting immediately struck him as a romantic event. "A helpless girl, overwhelmed with grief, left to the mercy of coarse, riotous peasants! And what a strange fate sent me here! What gentleness and nobility there are in her features and expression!" he thought as he looked at her and listened to her timid story.

When she began telling him that all this had happened the day after her father's funeral, her voice trembled. She turned away, and then, as if fearing he might take her words as meant to arouse his pity, looked at him with an apprehensive, questioning glance. There were tears in Rostov's eyes. Princess Mary noticed this and looked at him gratefully with that radiant gaze which made the plainness of her face disappear.

"I cannot express, Princess, how glad I am that I happened to ride this way and am able to serve you," said Rostov, rising. "Go whenever you please, and I give you my word of honor that no one shall dare cause you trouble if only you will allow me to act as your escort." And bowing respectfully, as if to a lady of royal blood, he moved toward the door.
Rostov's deferential tone seemed to say that though he would consider himself fortunate to know her, he did not wish to take advantage of her misfortune to impose himself.
Princess Mary understood this and appreciated his delicacy.
"I am very, very grateful to you," she said in French, "but I hope it was all a misunderstanding and that no one is to blame." She suddenly began to cry.
"Excuse me!" she said.
Rostov, with a frown, bowed low again and left the room.
